THE MONTREAL YMCA'S LINGUISTIC POLICY IN THREE DOCUMENTS, 1975 / 1979 / 1981
and what each of them says about the camps

Read closely 2026-09-07. All three were held and all three were read_state
"skimmed"; the 1979 review was upgraded earlier the same day and this file
covers the two either side of it.

  1975  1975-09-15-the-y-and-the-montreal-fact   src_ymf_1975_09_15_the_y_and_the_montreal_fact
        "The Y and the Montreal Fact" — the policy itself
        TWO text files: eng 4,092 bytes, fr 4,572. THE REPO HAD CACHED ONLY THE
        ENGLISH. Another instance of rule 50 (f_5427), found by checking the
        item's file list before reading rather than after.

  1979  1979-the-montreal-fact-75-79            src_ymf_1979_the_montreal_fact_75_79
        "The Montreal Fact '75-'79" — the four-year review (read earlier today)

  1981  1981-06-09-la-politique-linguistique    src_ymf_1981_06_09_la_politique_linguistique
        "La politique linguistique — Deuxième étape", "RAPPORT DU COMITÉ
        D'ORIENTATION LINGUISTIQUE", 29,233 bytes, French only, single text file

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1975: THE POLICY, AND ITS OWN DEADLINE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  "THE Y AND THE MONTREAL FACT / APPROVED SEPTEMBER 15, 1975 BY THE METROPOLITAN
  BOARD OF DIRECTORS / YMCA OF MONTREAL"

  "OBJECTIVES. A) TO ATTAIN A POSITION BY 1979 OR EARLIER WHEREBY THE ASSOCIATION
  IN ITS PROGRAM DELIVERY AND ITS SOCIAL MISSION IS REFLECTIVE OF THE TWO MAJOR
  CULTURES OF THE MONTREAL MILIEU WHILE MAINTAINING A SENSITIVITY TO THE
  ASPIRATIONS AND NEEDS OF OTHER CULTURAL SEGMENTS. B) TO CONDUCT THE PUBLIC AND
  INTERNAL AFFAIRS OF THE ASSOCIATION IN FRENCH AND ENGLISH."

THAT EXPLAINS WHY A REVIEW EXISTS IN 1979: it is the policy's own target year,
written into the objective. The 1979 document is not a retrospective someone
chose to write, it is a deadline coming due.

Strategy under STAFFING: bilingual ability "or the willingness to gain the
skills" made "of significant importance for positions where bilingualism is
designated as necessary"; attention in recruitment "to their cultural
background as future developments will require staff indigenous to the two
predominent cultures" [sic]; a French and English language training programme to
proceed "immediately on a priority basis"; and — with a date on it —
"EFFECTIVE JUNE 1976 ALL PUBLICATIONS DIRECTED TO ASSOCIATION WIDE GROUPS OF
LAYMEN AND STAFF MUST BE PUBLISHED IN BOTH LANGUAGES."

NULL RESULT, RUN IN BOTH LANGUAGES: "camp" occurs ZERO times in the English text
and ZERO in the French. Kanawana, Otoreke and Weredale likewise. THE POLICY THAT
GOVERNED THE CAMPS FOR THE NEXT DECADE DOES NOT MENTION CAMPS AT ALL. It is a
staffing, governance, planning and public-image document. The camps appear only
when the Association starts reporting on the policy, four years later.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1981: THE SECOND STAGE, AND THE ONLY HARD NUMBERS ANY OF THE THREE CARRY
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The camp paragraph is reprinted from 1979 essentially word for word in French:

  "Les camps de vacances du YMCA se veulent aussi représentatifs des milieux à
  desservir. Ainsi, le camp Otereke [sic], à Sainte-Agathe, permet à des
  familles francophones à faible revenu de passer de belles vacances en plein
  air. Le camp Weredale, au lac l'Achigan, se donne une vocation précise: être
  un camp de vacances français capable aussi de desservir les participants
  anglophones."

And the camps appear again in the report's summary of what the policy achieved:

  "Le YMCA a ouvert de nouvelles succursales en milieux francophone ou bilingue.
  a) Succursales Rive-Sud, Saint-Laurent, Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, Pointe
  Saint-Charles. b) CAMPS DE VACANCES: WEREDALE, OTOREKE."

So by 1981 the two camps are listed, beside four branches, as the Association's
francophone and bilingual establishments. KANAWANA IS AGAIN ABSENT — "Kanawana"
occurs ZERO times in the 29,233-character document.

THE NUMBERS, which neither of the other two documents gives:

  Francophone share of participants   28% (1975)  →  35% (1977)  →  50%
  Programmes delivered in French      36%
  Programmes delivered in English     37%
  Programmes delivered bilingually    27%
     stated aim: "50% en anglais, 50% en français"
  Advertisements English-only         83% (1975)  →  12% (1979)
  Internal notices English-only       97% (1975)  →  35% (1979)

The candour is worth noting in a document of this kind. The section carrying the
programme figures is headed "LES PROGRAMMES NE RÉPONDENT PAS COMPLÈTEMENT À NOS
ATTENTES" — the programmes do not fully meet our expectations — and the report
sets the gap out rather than burying it: half the participants are francophone
and about a third of the programmes are in French.

Also new since 1979: a Pointe Saint-Charles branch in the list, and
Hochelaga-Maisonneuve now described as "une succursale ENTIÈREMENT FRANCOPHONE."
Signage is being done "selon les règlements émis par le gouvernement (Charte de
la langue française)" — the Charter named directly. And a consequence the
Association is pleased with: "d'autres organismes d'expression française font
appel à notre expertise," with invitations to government consultations alongside
the Ville de Montréal, Centraide and the Fédération des centres communautaires.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WHAT THE THREE TOGETHER SETTLE, AND WHAT THEY DO NOT
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SETTLED: the policy has a date (15 September 1975), a board (the Metropolitan
Board of Directors), a deadline written into its own objective (1979), a
publications deadline (June 1976), a measurable outcome (28% → 50% francophone
participation), and an admitted shortfall (36% of programmes in French).

NOT SETTLED, AND NOT TO BE INFERRED: why Kanawana is absent from all three.
The 1975 policy names no camp at all, so its absence there means nothing. Its
absence from the 1979 and 1981 achievement lists is consistent with several
readings — that Kanawana was already anglophone and stayed so; that it was not
thought to need changing; that its francophone work (the 1969 "Living-in-French"
section, recorded in traditions/french-language-camping.md) predated the policy
and was not counted as an achievement of it. NOTHING HERE CHOOSES BETWEEN THOSE.
What the documents establish is only where the Association pointed when asked
what it had done, and it pointed at Otoreke and Weredale.
